question: What work did you do for the Post Office when you were at Ernst & Young?
You joined the Post Office in September 2003 and left in March 2016, and so served in the Post Office for 13 years?
Your work as Head of Risk and Control and, as we've said, that was from September 2003 until June 2006. What was the nature of your role as Head of Risk and Control?
Did you attend board meetings of Post Office Limited?
What was the Branch Audit Team?
When you joined, was it striking to you that the Post Office did not have a risk, audit or compliance committee?
Did it ever occur to you or anyone else that applied their brain to the issue that the losses might not be caused by postmaster conduct?
What research or inquiry did you undertake to determine whether the Horizon System should be on the risk register or should not be on the risk register?
Was there any, in your three years in this post, discussion about Fujitsu employees having unrestricted and unauditable access to the Post Office Horizon System?

Was there, in your time, in the three years that you held this role, a policy document that governed the way in which audits were to be conducted, for example the need to keep an open mind and the duty to follow all reasonable lines of investigation?
Can you recall a phrase in this period, namely "ARQ data"?
As well as financial auditing, did Ernst & Young produce service audit reports that concerned the Horizon processing environment?
What did the role of Head of P&BA involve when you took it over?
Would you agree that internal auditors would be a vital source of assurance within the corporation?
The position had changed. You were now looking to conduct a general due diligence exercise, which would "confirm our belief in the robustness of the system". That's what you did, wasn't it?
You were aware by this time about the Callendar Square bug, weren't you?
By this time, there were ten bugs that were known about. I want to understand whether you knew about them: a bug called the receipts and payments mismatch bug?
On what basis did you remain satisfied that all money that was missing had been stolen?

You now know that the Horizon System was significantly compromised by a series of bugs, errors and defects that had been the effect of causing accounting discrepancies that were wrongly attributed to the criminal actions of subpostmasters that led, in some cases, to their conviction and imprisonment. With the benefit of reflection, do you agree that the decision not to commission a fully independent investigation and audit of the Horizon System in 2010 and, instead, for you to prepare a report that had as its object to demonstrate the robustness and reliability of Horizon, was a crass mistake?
What were the "compassionate factors" that were borne in mind?
